name: Hiking
seoDesc: Hiking: work out trail average grade from the distance and the elevation gain. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Hiking calculator the distance, the elevation gain, the hiker's weight and the backpack weight and it returns trail average grade. Think of it as a shortcut for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Hiking calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hiking calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports trail average grade in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the distance, the elevation gain, the hiker's weight and the backpack weight.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hiking calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Trail average grade=elevation gain ÷ the square root of ((distance ^ 2) − (elevation gain ^ 2))
Weight lost=((1 ÷ 7700) × ((330693 ÷ 30577460000) × distance × (5610 × (trail average grade ^ 5) × backpack weight + 8415 × (trail average grade ^ 5) × hiker's weight − 1174 × (trail average grade ^ 4) × backpack weight − 1761 × (trail average grade ^ 4) × hiker's weight − 1536 × (trail average grade ^ 3) × backpack weight − 2304 × (trail average grade ^ 3) × hiker's weight + 1038 × (trail average grade ^ 2) × backpack weight + 1557 × (trail average grade ^ 2) × hiker's weight + 392 × trail average grade × backpack weight + 588 × trail average grade × hiker's weight + 50 × backpack weight + 75 × hiker's weight)))
Calories burned=((330693 ÷ 30577460000) × distance × (5610 × (trail average grade ^ 5) × backpack weight + 8415 × (trail average grade ^ 5) × hiker's weight − 1174 × (trail average grade ^ 4) × backpack weight − 1761 × (trail average grade ^ 4) × hiker's weight − 1536 × (trail average grade ^ 3) × backpack weight − 2304 × (trail average grade ^ 3) × hiker's weight + 1038 × (trail average grade ^ 2) × backpack weight + 1557 × (trail average grade ^ 2) × hiker's weight + 392 × trail average grade × backpack weight + 588 × trail average grade × hiker's weight + 50 × backpack weight + 75 × hiker's weight))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilocalories, and convertible to any of the 33 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in meters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Energy, opening in kilocalories
  • Mass, opening in kilograms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hiking calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the distance, the elevation gain and the hiker's weight — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hiking calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns trail average grade, derived from the distance, the elevation gain and the hiker's weight. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hiking calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance, the elevation gain, the hiker's weight and the backpack weight, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Hiking calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
